title: Dog handling, leash and group walking
audience: Dog walkers who handle individual dogs and groups on leads in streets, parks and other public places
referencesAtStart: Official sources: City of Port Phillip, Do I need a dog walking permit? (Dog walkers) (no date shown); City of Yarra, Commercial dog walkers (no date shown); City of Ryde, Application for dog minding (open space) form (July 2026, form footer); Agriculture Victoria, Code of Practice for the Operation of Boarding Establishments (revision 1, updated October 2004; printed April 2025), which applies to boarding establishments only.
learningOutcomes: Handle a dog on a lead with control, and keep each dog under effective control in public
Set group limits for each walker and each place, using the council and business limits
Recognise the signs of stress or aggression in a dog and separate it from the group before harm occurs

instruction.heading: Control on the lead and under effective control
instruction.body: A dog on a lead must be under the walker's control at all times. Port Phillip's dog walker page (no date shown) asks for dogs to be under effective control, asks handlers to carry a chain, cord or leash for each dog, and requires each dog to wear a collar or harness with the council's identification marker. Those are council-specific requirements that apply in Port Phillip. The principle of control is good practice everywhere. Use a lead of a length and type that lets you hold the dog without being pulled off balance. Do not wrap the lead around your hand or wrist. Keep the dog beside you or behind you where possible, and check the road, the footpath and the verge before crossing. Section 6.1 of the Victorian boarding code (revision 1, updated October 2004, printed April 2025) allows dogs to be walked on roads only when several conditions are met. Those include keeping every dog leashed the whole time, having an adult supervisor who is at least 17, no more than two dogs per person, and the owner's written approval. The business should adopt them as good practice and confirm the position.

instruction.heading: Group limits and the council rules
instruction.body: A walker with a group of dogs is taking on a risk that grows with each dog. Port Phillip's dog walker page (no date shown) requires a permit when a walker handles four or more dogs at one time, and sets a limit of eight dogs per person and twelve dogs in total across all handlers. Yarra's page (no date shown) caps the number of animals one person may exercise at one time at four. Ryde's form (July 2026) allows up to four dogs under a commercial minder permit. These are council-specific figures and apply in those councils only. The business limit must be set at or below the lowest limit that applies to the walk, and it must be recorded in {{business:procedures.approved_sop}}. Where the walk crosses a council boundary, the lower limit of the two councils applies to the walk as a whole.

instruction.heading: Reading the dog and separating before harm
instruction.body: A dog that is stressed may pant, yawn, lip-lick, turn its head away, lower its tail, stiffen, freeze or hide. A dog showing aggression may growl, bare its teeth, raise its hackles, stare or lunge. Watch for these signs before a conflict starts. Move the dog away from the trigger, such as another dog, a child, a bicycle or a loud noise, and do not force the dog past it. In a group, keep dogs that do not get along apart and walk them separately. Never grab a fight between dogs by the collar or the body, because you can be bitten. Record each incident, including the dogs involved, the time and the action taken. The bite prevention and emergency steps are in “Bite prevention and emergency response”, and the business's group-walk procedure is held in {{business:procedures.approved_sop}}.

procedure: Check each dog's temperament and the client's notes before the walk, and separate any dog that does not get along with the group
Check the lead, collar or harness, and the council tag, before leaving the home
Confirm the council permit and group limit for each place on the route, and use the lowest limit that applies
Hold each dog on a lead of suitable length, and keep the dogs under effective control at all times
Watch for stress and aggression signs, and move the dog away from the trigger before a conflict starts
Record each walk, the dogs walked, the place and any incident, and return each dog to the client at the agreed time

workedExamples.situation: A walker has five dogs booked for a walk through a Port Phillip park. One dog starts to growl and lunge at a bicycle, and the walker has the leads wrapped around one hand.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should the walker do first?
workedExamples.reasoning: Port Phillip sets its permit trigger at four or more dogs, so five dogs means the walker must hold the permit. Five dogs is within the council's limit of eight per walker, but only if the permit is held and the walker keeps control. The first action is to free the leads from the wrapped hand, move the growling dog away from the bicycle, and keep the other dogs under control. The walker should not force the dog past the trigger. The walk should be shortened or the group reduced if control is lost, and the incident recorded.

workedExamples.situation: A walk crosses from one council into another. The first council allows four dogs and the second allows eight.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How many dogs can be walked for the whole route?
workedExamples.reasoning: The walk must stay within the lower limit that applies to any part of the route. The walker should plan the route so that the group does not exceed four dogs at any time in either council, or should split the group and walk the sections separately. The limit should be recorded before the walk.

equipmentAndPpe: Leads of a suitable length and type, checked before each walk
Collars or harnesses, checked for fit and wear
Council tag for each dog, where the council requires one
Gloves for handling leads and dogs where the business procedure requires them
Water and a towel for each walk, for the dogs and the walker

commonErrors.error: Wrapping the lead around the hand or wrist.
commonErrors.prevention: Hold the lead in the hand with the loop released, so that a sudden pull does not trap the hand.

commonErrors.error: Walking more dogs than the council limit allows.
commonErrors.prevention: Set the limit at the lowest applicable council limit before the walk, and split the group where needed.

commonErrors.error: Grabbing a fight between dogs by the collar or body.
commonErrors.prevention: Separate the dogs with a barrier or by moving the group away, and do not put your hands between them.

commonErrors.error: Walking a known aggressive dog with the group.
commonErrors.prevention: Walk the dog separately, and record the temperament note on the client record.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Port Phillip requires dogs to be under effective control, handlers to carry a chain, cord or leash, and each dog to wear a council identification marker. These apply in Port Phillip only.

Permit threshold by council: in City of Port Phillip, a dog walking permit is needed to walk four or more dogs at a time. With a permit, the maximum is eight dogs per person and twelve dogs in total, whatever the number of handlers. In City of Yarra, without a permit no more than four dogs or other animals may be exercised by one person at any one time. In City of Ryde, a commercial dog minder permit covers minding up to four dogs in off-leash areas. Work above these limits needs the council permit. All of these limits are council-specific.
Section 6.1 of the Victorian boarding code sets conditions for walking dogs on roads.
Completing this lesson does not grant a permit for a group walk or a dog-handling authority.

qualityStandard: Every walk uses a group limit at or below the lowest applicable council limit
Every dog is on a lead and under effective control on public land
Every dog that does not get along with the group is walked separately
Every incident is recorded with the dogs, time and action
documentationEvidence: Walk record with dogs walked, place, group size and times
Incident record for any growl, lunge, bite or fight
Temperament notes for each dog, on the client record
Council permit and group limit recorded for each route
summary: Keep every dog on a lead and under effective control in public
Use the lowest applicable council group limit, and split the group where needed
Watch for stress and aggression signs, and separate dogs before harm occurs
Council limits are specific to each council.

Council limits apply only in the named councils.

knowledgeChecks.question: A dog starts to growl and lunge at a bicycle during a group walk. What is the first action?
options: Let the dog run it off, so the group stays calm and nobody is hurt, since the bicycle will soon pass by
Move the dog away from the trigger and keep the group under control, without forcing the dog past it
Grab the dog's collar and pull it past the bicycle, so the walk can continue with the group on the route

knowledgeChecks.question: A walk crosses from a council allowing four dogs into a council allowing eight. What group limit applies to the whole route?
options: Eight, the higher of the two
Twelve, because it is the Port Phillip total
Four, the lower limit of the two councils

knowledgeChecks.question: How must a dog on a lead be controlled, according to this lesson?
options: Under the walker's control at all times
Off the lead when the path is quiet
At the walker's discretion when other dogs are near
